texts.facts: This is a criminal revision petition u/s 438 of BNSS filed against order dated 31.05.2023 passed by the court of Ld. Metropolitan Magistrate (NI Act) Digital Court-02, NI Act, SED in Criminal Complaint No. 10864/2022 titled as M/s Indo Spirits Vs. M/s Sakriya Technologies Pvt. Ltd, whereby the revisionists were summoned to face trial for the commission of offence punishable u/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act (hereinafter referred to as '138 NI Act'). The said complaint was filed by the respondent against the revisionists and some others alleging commission of offence punishable u/s 138 NI Act. GROUNDS OF REVISION 2. Ld. Counsel for the revisionist submits that the impugned order is liable to be [LEAKAGE_MASK] on the following grounds:- A. BECAUSE the Order dated 31.05.2023 passed by the Court of the Ld. MM(NI. ACT) Digital Court-02, SED, Saket Courts is bad in law, an abuse of the process of law and deserves to be [LEAKAGE_MASK] by this Hon'ble Court. BECAUSE the Ld. MM(NI. ACT) Digital Court-02, SED, Saket Courts failed to appreciate that even the case of the respondent was that the legal demand notice was delivered on 05.09.2023/06.09.2023 and the present complaint filed on 31.10.2022 which was barred by limitation and as per the mandate of Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 the Ld. MM(NI. ACT) Digital Court-02, SED, Saket Courts could not have taken cognizance of the same. Copy of Case status of CC No. Crl. Revision No: 224/2025 Rahul Raithi vs M/s Indo Spirit page no. 3 of 25 10864/2022 as available on ecourt website is annexed herewith as Annexure P-5. C. BECAUSE as per the mandate of Section 142(1)(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881: 142. Cognizance of offences.- (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974)- (a)no court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 138 except upon a complaint, in writing, made by the payee or, as the case may be, the holder in due course of the cheque; (b)such complaint is made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138: As the time under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 time period of 15 days to make payment in pursuance of the legal demand notice ended on 21.09.2022, the complaint should have been filed within a month which expired on 22.10.2022 admittedly the same was not done and the complaint as filed on 31.10.2022 was time barred. The Respondent had also not filed any application seeking condonation of delay and the delay has also not been condoned by the Ld. MM(NI. ACT) Digital Court-02, SED, Saket Courts vide the impugned summoning order. Revision No: 224/2025 Rahul Raithi vs M/s Indo Spirit page no. 4 of 25 and 06.09.2022 and this complaint was filed on 31.10.2022, thus the same has been filed within limitation." Whereas the demand notice as per the complaint was delivered on 05.09.2022. The limitation period also expired on 22.10.2022 and the complaint filed on 31.10.2022 was barred by limitation. E. BECAUSE the impugned order on the face of it shows total non-application of mind by the Ld. MM. The dates as mentioned in the order also reveal that the same was barred by limitation but the Ld. MM has termed that as filed within limitation. BECAUSE the Ld. MM failed to appreciate that the petitioners were not even authorised signatories in the impugned cheque and as per the board resolution were only authorised to sign all agreements, power of attorney, documents, writings, applications, indemnities, applications / online undertakings, correspondences/applications for retail vends (L-7V) with Excise Department, GNCTD. The same was in terms of the Delhi Excise Policy 2021-22. The same does not make them liable for day to day operations or responsible for the company.

The law regarding the liability of directors of a company was dealt with and expounded by the Hon'ble Supreme Court firstly in S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. vs. Neeta Bhalla and Another, (2005) 8 SCC 89. The relevant part of the observations is reproduced below :- "...(a) It is necessary to specifically aver in a complaint un- der Section 141 that at the time the offence was commit- ted, the person accused was in charge of, and responsible for the conduct of business of the company. A director in a company cannot be deemed to be in charge of and responsible to the company for conduct of its business. (c) ...The question notes that the Managing Director or Joint Managing Director would be admittedly in charge of the company and responsible to the company for conduct of its business. So far as signatory of a cheque which is dishonoured is con- cerned, he is clearly responsible for the incriminating act and will be covered under sub-section (2) of Section 141..." 11. In K.K.Ahuja V. V.K. Vohra (2009) 10 SCC 48, the Hon'ble Supreme Court had summarised the position under Section 141 as un- der: "20. The position under section 141 of the Act can be sum- marized thus : (ii) In the case of a director or an officer of the company who signed the cheque on behalf of the company, there is no need to make a specific averment that he was in charge of and was responsible to the company, for the conduct of the business of the company or make any specific allegation about consent, connivance or negligence. (iii) In the case of a Director, Secretary or Manager (as de- fined in Sec. 2(24) of the Companies Act) or a person re- ferred to in clauses (e) and (f) of section 5 of Companies Act, an averment in the complaint that he was in charge of, and was responsible to the company, for the conduct of the business of the company is necessary to bring the case un- der section 141(1). (iv) Other Officers of a company can not be made liable un- der sub-section (1) of section 141. Other officers of a com- pany can be made liable only under sub-section (2) of Section 141, be averring in the complaint their position and duties in the company and their role in regard to the is- sue and dishonour of the cheque, disclosing consent, con- nivance or negligence..." 12. On similar lines, the Honble Apex Court in National Small Industries Corp. Ltd. V. Harmeet Singh Paintal (2010) 3 SCC 330 carved out the following principles: Crl. From the above discussion, the following principles emerge: (i) The primary responsibility is on the complainant to make specific averments as are required under the law in the complaint so as to make the accused vicariously liable. For fastening the criminal liability, there is no presumption that every Director knows about the transaction. (ii) Section 141 does not make all the Directors liable for the offence. (iii) Vicarious liability can be inferred against a company registered or incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 only if the requisite statements, which are required to be averred in the complaint/petition, are made so as to make the accused therein vicariously liable for offence commit- ted by the company along with averments in the petition containing that the accused were in charge of and respon- sible for the business of the company and by virtue of their position they are liable to be proceeded with.
